steps: Each circle is cut by strip edges into pieces. A piece can join only a matching piece of the same size at the same height.
Note each arc: its height on the strip, its size, and which edge it touches.
Pair arcs that complete each other, and count circles that sit fully inside one strip.
The best arrangement gives 7 complete circles.
qs.trap: Joining arcs of different sizes, or at different heights. Strips cannot be moved up or down.

steps: Number the small regions first, so you can name each triangle by its parts.
Count single-region triangles, then triangles made of two regions, then three or more.
Check every corner where three lines meet: each can start a triangle.
The total is 24.
qs.trap: Counting four-sided regions as triangles. Check that each shape has exactly three straight sides.

steps: Each piece carries part of a digit on a grey background.
Find the pieces with the outer edges of the number first: left curves and right curves.
Join pieces whose black strokes continue across the edges.
The digits read 8, 5, 6, 3.
qs.trap: Reading a 6 as an 8 or a 5 as a 3. Check the openings of each digit before deciding.

steps: Use the symmetry: count the surfaces of one arm carefully, then multiply by 4.
Count the central block's top and side faces separately.
Add the single flat base.
The total is 72.
qs.trap: Counting only visible faces. Symmetry tells you the hidden arms are the same as the visible ones.

steps: The three cuts make 8 pieces: 4 cone tips on top and 4 lower pieces (part cone, part slab).
Each tip: curved surface, two upright cut faces, one flat bottom: 4 surfaces.
Each lower piece: level cut face, curved surface, two upright cut faces, slab top, two slab sides, slab bottom: 8 surfaces.

steps: A pair needs the same design (same star colour) and opposite sides: one left, one right.
Turn each shoe in your mind until its toe points the same way, then check which side its laces and heel are on.
Group shoes by star colour, then pair lefts with rights in each group.
There are 4 complete pairs.
qs.trap: Pairing two left shoes because they look alike. Rotate one: if it overlaps the other exactly, it is the same foot.

steps: Count all corners as if the patches were separate: 12 × 5 + 20 × 6 = 180.
At every junction of a football, exactly 3 patches meet.
So the real number of vertices is 180 ÷ 3 = 60.
Check with Euler: faces 32, edges 90, vertices 60: 60 − 90 + 32 = 2.

steps: Wheels 2 and 3 lie on a radius of the circle, so the centre of the vehicle is at 525 + 85 = 610 cm.
Wheel-1 is on the centre line of the vehicle, ahead of the middle. From Wheel-2 it is 85 across and some distance along.
Along: square root of (180² − 85²) = square root of 25,175, about 158.7 cm.
Radius = square root of (610² + 158.7²), about 630 cm: inside the range.

steps: Radius = 18.85 ÷ (2 × 3.14), about 3 cm.
The circle just fits inside the hexagon at the centre of the star, so the hexagon's inner radius is 3 cm.
Hexagon side = 2 × 3 ÷ 1.732, about 3.46 cm. Each star point is an equilateral triangle with this side.
Area = 0.433 × 3.46², about 5.20 cm².

steps: No plank can be taller than 30 cm, so 3 planks reach at most 90 cm. You need at least 4.
Cut the 20 cm side into 4: each plank is 10 × 5 × 30 cm.
Stand three planks on their 30 cm side and lay one on its 10 cm side: 30 + 30 + 30 + 10 = 100.
Volume = 10 × 5 × 30 = 1500 cm³ (the block's 6000 ÷ 4).

steps: Upright stacks: 4 + 0.5 × 4 = 6 cm, so 5 cups per stack, 4 × 3 = 12 stacks, 60 cups.
Lying down: a stack along the 16 cm side holds n cups as long as 4 + 0.5(n − 1) is at most 16, so n = 25.
Across the 12 cm width, 3 stacks fit side by side (the box is 6 cm high, so one layer).
3 × 25 = 75 cups, more than standing them up.

steps: The middle sphere sits at the centre of the tetrahedron and touches all four corner spheres.
Centre to corner = side × root 6 ÷ 4 = 120 × 0.612, about 73.5 cm.
Subtract the corner sphere's radius: 73.5 − 40 = 33.5 cm.
Note: the key measures the gap between the spheres. The tetrahedron's flat faces are only 24.5 cm from its centre, so they are not treated as walls.

steps: Opposite faces of a die add up to 7 (1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4). Section P shows how the faces sit around each die.
For each die, list which faces are hidden: on the table, against another die, or under a die.
To make the visible sum as large as possible, put the smallest numbers on the hidden faces.
Add the visible faces of all ten dice: the maximum is 141.
qs.trap: Forgetting that opposite faces add to 7. If 1 is hidden at the bottom, 6 must be on top.

steps: Check each tile: where its path enters and leaves.
Since tiles cannot rotate, each tile only links certain directions.
Build a path from A, alternating tile types and making sure every type is used once.
The shortest valid path uses 12 tiles; the key also accepts 13.
qs.trap: Rotating a tile in your head to make it fit. The rules say tiles keep their orientation.

steps: Stars differ by the number of arms (5, 6, 7, 8) and arm shape (thin, rounded).
List the star types in the main image first.
Check each option star by star against your list.
A and C contain stars that are not in the image.
qs.trap: Forgetting that the question asks for stars NOT in the image.

steps: The clues fit a clockwise order of 8 positions: A at 6, B at 7:30, C at 9, then on round, starting again after H.
So a letter's position = its number (A = 0) divided by 8; the remainder tells the spot.
GOA: G at 3, O at 3, A at 6. True. SKY: S at 9, K at 9, Y at 6. True.
FLY: F is at 1:30, not 3. BYE: B is at 7:30, not 9. Both false.

steps: Choose distinctive pieces: crosses, sharp corners, short curves.
Find each fragment in the original, at the same angle and size.
Every fragment in an option must appear exactly; one wrong piece rules it out.
B and D contain only exact fragments.
qs.trap: Accepting a fragment that is slightly rotated or mirrored.

steps: A handpump lifts a piston with a one-way valve. The handle is a lever: handle down, piston up.
On the up-stroke the piston lifts water above it and opens the bottom valve to suck more water in.
On the down-stroke the bottom valve closes and the piston valve opens, so water passes above the piston.
A and B show the handle, piston and water levels correctly matched.
qs.trap: Forgetting the lever: pushing the handle down lifts the piston.

steps: A scissor arm folds flat only if every joint can turn and no link forms a fixed triangle.
Check the ends: where the last links meet and where they slide on the wall track.
A fixed triangle or a locked end stops the folding part way.
B and D can fold completely.
qs.trap: Looking only at the middle links. The joints at the two ends decide whether the arm can fold flat.

steps: Pick a unique feature, such as the red block's step, and note its position relative to the green blocks.
Turn each option until that feature lines up.
Check the second feature, such as the cut in the orange disc.
A, B and C are the same object; D is not.
qs.trap: Matching colours only. Check positions and shapes as well.

steps: Pigment (paint) primaries are red, yellow and blue.
Each secondary sits between the two primaries that make it: orange between red and yellow, and so on.
Complementary colours sit opposite each other.
A and D follow these rules; B and C break the order.

steps: Lap time = circumference ÷ speed = 2 × pi × radius ÷ speed.
Yellow: 3pi s. Green: 3pi s. Same lap time, so they keep the same angle apart and never overtake: A is true.
Red: 8pi s; blue: 6pi s. Different, so B is false. C is false (equal times).
In 3 blue laps (18pi s) red does 2.25 laps: blue gains only 270° and passes red once, so D is false.

X has wide, even rings: steady, healthy growth (A and B true).
Y has narrow, uneven rings: some years were bad, likely due to drought, cold or poor soil (C true).
So D is false.

The bite marks show where the small sphere cut: their position and size along the strip.
Compare with the top and front views: where the small sphere touches the big one, and how deep.
A and D place the small sphere so it cuts exactly those segments.
qs.trap: Ignoring the front view. The top view alone cannot show how high the cut is.

steps: In perspective, nearer objects look bigger. Rings of equal real thickness look thicker when nearer.
Ring 1 looks thickest, so it is nearest (C true).
Rings 2 and 4 look equally thin, so they are at the same distance (B true).
Rings 6 and 3 look thicker than 5, so they are closer (A true). 5 is not the farthest, so D is false.

steps: A stamp prints the mirror image of its face.
Mirror the stamp face left to right and read the print.
The stamp can also be turned, so rotated versions of the print are possible.
A, B and D are correct prints (some rotated); C has a letter that would not appear.
qs.trap: Reading the stamp face directly. The print is always a mirror image.

Check each option: does the top edge fit the bottom edge, and the left fit the right?
Tiles may need to shift by half a tile, as X does in Y.
B and C fit together without gaps; A and D leave gaps.
qs.trap: Judging by how "nice" the shape is. Only matching edges matter.

D: singers and actors are both performers, and some people are both. Fits.
B: not all designers are men. C: cats are inside mammals, so the circles nest rather than overlap.

steps: The strip repeats one unit across its length.
Pick a clear feature in each option: a hook, a T-junction, a gap.
Find it in the strip and compare square by square around it.
A and C match parts of the strip; B and D are altered or mirrored.
qs.trap: Accepting a mirrored copy, which looks very similar.

steps: A flip about the vertical axis mirrors left and right.
A 180° turn then flips both left-right and top-bottom.
The two left-right changes cancel, leaving only an upside-down flip.
So the result is the planet mirrored top to bottom: option C.

qs.trap: Doing the 180° turn as a second left-right flip. A half-turn changes both directions.

steps: In animation, frames are close together where the motion is slow and far apart where it is fast.
Watch where the bee speeds up and slows down along the path.
Find the option whose frame spacing matches that change of speed.
Option D matches.
qs.trap: Choosing evenly spaced frames. Real motion speeds up and slows down.

steps: Look at each quarter separately: corner square or quarter circle, and which way it faces.
Track how each quarter changes from figure to figure.
Apply the same change to get the next figure.
Option B follows the rule.
qs.trap: Treating the shape as a whole. Quarter by quarter is far easier.

steps: The pen has a distinct cap, clip and long barrel with a rounded end.
Find the pieces that make the clip and the rounded end first.
Check that the remaining pieces fill the barrel without gaps or extra bits.
Set B fits exactly.
qs.trap: Accepting a set with one extra or missing piece. Every piece must be used.

steps: Read the grid row by row and column by column: the black shape changes one way, the red square another.
Find the rule for each direction.
Work out what each gap must hold from both its row and its column.
Option C fits all three gaps.
qs.trap: Checking only the row. Each gap must fit its column as well.

steps: A building block is the smallest piece that, repeated, makes the whole pattern.
Find one full repeat of the colour order in the pattern.
Note the lengths and offsets of the bars, not just their colours.
Option C repeats to give the pattern exactly.
qs.trap: Matching colours but not bar lengths or offsets.

steps: Rank the slices by size: orange, white, green, yellow, then the small blue and purple.
Estimate rough shares: orange and white about a quarter each, green and yellow a little less.
The bars must follow the same order and roughly the same ratios.
Only D has the right order and proportions.
qs.trap: Checking only the biggest bar. The small bars (blue, purple) also decide.

steps: Shutter speed is how long the shutter stays open.
A slower shutter lets light in for longer: a brighter photo.
The size of the opening is the aperture (A). Sensor sensitivity is ISO (B).
Pixel count is resolution (D), not exposure.
qs.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 234 85" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="2" y="2" width="230" height="20" rx="3" fill="#DCE6F7" stroke="none" stroke-width="0"/><text x="8" y="16" font-family="Plus Jakarta Sans, sans-serif" font-size="8.4" font-weight="700" fill="#0A2560" text-anchor="start">Control</text><text x="98" y="16" font-family="Plus Jakarta Sans, sans-serif" font-size="8.4" font-weight="700" fill="#0A2560" text-anchor="start">What it changes</text><text x="8" y="37" font-family="Plus Jakarta Sans, sans-serif" font-size="8.2" font-weight="700" fill="#0A2560" text-anchor="start">Aperture</text><text x="98" y="37" font-family="Plus Jakarta Sans, sans-serif" font-size="8.2" font-weight="600" fill="#5A6278" text-anchor="start">size of the opening</text><line x1="2" y1="42" x2="232" y2="42" stroke="#E8DFC8" stroke-width="0.6" stroke-linecap="round" /><rect x="2" y="43" width="230" height="18" rx="2" fill="#DDF0E6" stroke="none" stroke-width="0"/><text x="8" y="56" font-family="Plus Jakarta Sans, sans-serif" font-size="8.2" font-weight="700" fill="#0A2560" text-anchor="start">Shutter speed</text><text x="98" y="56" font-family="Plus Jakarta Sans, sans-serif" font-size="8.2" font-weight="600" fill="#5A6278" text-anchor="start">time the light enters</text><line x1="2" y1="61" x2="232" y2="61" stroke="#E8DFC8" stroke-width="0.6" stroke-linecap="round" /><text x="8" y="75" font-family="Plus Jakarta Sans, sans-serif" font-size="8.2" font-weight="700" fill="#0A2560" text-anchor="start">ISO</text><text x="98" y="75" font-family="Plus Jakarta Sans, sans-serif" font-size="8.2" font-weight="600" fill="#5A6278" text-anchor="start">sensor sensitivity</text><line x1="2" y1="80" x2="232" y2="80" stroke="#E8DFC8" stroke-width="0.6" stroke-linecap="round" /></svg>
qs.trap: Mixing up shutter and aperture. Shutter = time; aperture = size of the hole.

steps: Each visible edge of the folded shape is either an original edge or a fold.
Colours show which side faces up: red means the flap was turned over.
Unfold one flap at a time and draw where its fold line sits on the square.
Option A shows the fold lines in the right places and angles.
qs.trap: Ignoring the colours, which tell you which flaps were folded over.

steps: Animators use standard mouth shapes: closed for M, B and P; teeth showing for T and D; round for O.
Read each frame and match it to a sound.
Count the sounds and compare with each sentence.
"Today is my day!" matches the sequence.
qs.trap: Matching only the first frame. Check the whole sentence.

steps: All shadows point the same way and have the same length, because the light rays are parallel.
A cube casts a full square-ended shadow; a pyramid's shadow narrows to a point.
A triangular prism's shadow depends on which way its sloping face points.
Option D shows all three correctly.
qs.trap: Giving the shadows different directions. One light source, parallel rays: one direction.

steps: The rod's tip resists changes in motion (inertia).
When the ball starts moving, the tip lags behind and bends backwards.
At steady speed it straightens; when the ball stops, the tip carries on forward and wobbles.
Option A shows this sequence.
qs.trap: Expecting the rod to lean forward as the ball starts. The tip lags first.

steps: Compare the red, blue and purple grids in each row.
Find how the third grid relates to the first two: shared dots, different dots, or a count.
Check that the rule works for the second and third rows.
Apply it to the top row: option A.
qs.trap: Finding a rule from one row only. Always test it on the other rows.

steps: Look at the rows and columns around the gap.
Find the pattern in the half-shaded direction: up, down, left, right.
The missing block must continue the pattern in both directions.
Option A fits.
qs.trap: Matching only the row above. The row below and the columns also matter.

steps: Follow the stems and leaves that touch each edge of the gap.
Each must continue smoothly into the missing piece.
Check the leaf directions inside each option.
Option C continues every stem and leaf.
qs.trap: Picking the option that "looks similar". Edges must line up exactly.

steps: Put the strips back in order: the top and bottom strips show the letter tops and bottoms.
Identify shapes: A has a point, E has three bars, F two bars, H a middle bar.
Read letter by letter, left to right.
The word is AEFHIFTLEA.
qs.trap: Confusing E and F. E has a bottom bar; F does not.

steps: Compare each letter with its result: what is mirrored, removed or added.
Apply the same change to N.
Check the answer against both examples.
The official answer is B.
qs.trap: Seeing only one change. Make the rule work for both I and S.

steps: A wheelbarrow is a lever: the wheel is the fulcrum, the load is in the middle, the effort is at the handles.
Effort = load × (distance from wheel to load) ÷ (distance from wheel to handles).
The closer the wheel is to the load's centre, the smaller the effort.
D places the wheel closest under the load, so it needs the least effort.

qs.trap: Choosing the wheel at the very front. Moving the wheel under the load makes it easier.

steps: To hold the bike still, the force on the pedals must balance gravity pulling the bike back.
A small front chainring with a big rear cog (low gear) gives the biggest turning force at the wheel for the same foot force.
So low gear needs the least pedal force to balance the slope.
Option B shows that setting.

qs.trap: Choosing high gear because it is "stronger". High gear is for speed; low gear is for force.

steps: Find the features you can check from above: the stairs, the window opening, the slot at the front.
Note their positions relative to each other.
Compare each option feature by feature.
Only C matches every feature.
qs.trap: Checking only the big shapes. The small slot and steps decide between close options.

steps: Pick one corner where three faces meet in a view, and note how the blue shapes cross the edges.
Patterns must continue across edges that touch on the cube.
Fold each net in your mind and check that corner.
Only C keeps every pattern continuous.
qs.trap: Checking faces one at a time. The edges where patterns meet are the real test.

steps: Use the faulty results: left 90 › right 90; right 90 › left 45; right 45 › left 30; left 60 › right 30.
Measure headings clockwise from north. North-east = 45°.
90° is due East.

qs.trap: Using the captain's intended turns. The ship turns the faulty way every time.

steps: A cone's surface unwraps into part of a ring (a fan shape).
A spiral cut that goes once around the cone becomes a curved band on the fan.
Its width changes from one end to the other, because the cut moves up the cone.
Option A shows the correct curved band.
qs.trap: Expecting a straight band. Cone surfaces always unwrap into curves.

steps: Each position shows two pieces of the pattern through the cut-outs.
Combine the visible pieces from all four positions into one picture.
Check which option contains all those pieces in the right places.
Option D does.
qs.trap: Building the pattern from one or two positions only. All four must agree.

steps: "Visual grammar" means the same style rules: stroke contrast, angle and shape of curves.
The given letters are blackletter-style: thick and thin strokes from an angled broad nib, with sharp, broken curves.
Compare each "s" for the same contrast and angle.
Option B matches.

qs.trap: Picking a heavy "s" just because it is bold. Weight alone is not style.

steps: Unfold step by step, in reverse order.
Each unfold mirrors the cut across that fold line.
Three folds give the cut in 4 or more mirrored places.
Option A shows the cuts in the right mirrored positions.

qs.trap: Unfolding in the wrong order. Undo the last fold first.

steps: The first example shows the rule: place the shapes so the marked points meet.
Keep only the region covered by both shapes.
Do the same for the second pair.
The overlap matches option B.

qs.trap: Joining the shapes (union) instead of keeping the overlap.

steps: A worm crawls in waves: the body bunches up and then stretches out.
Look at the frames on either side of each gap.
The missing frame must be halfway between its neighbours.
Option B fits both gaps.
qs.trap: Choosing frames that repeat a neighbour. Each frame must show a small change.
